pos: n. (the Hessian imperial abbey founded 769 by Lull, where Luther preached on his way to Worms in 1521)
etymology: Old High German Haruolfesfeld, Haruolf's field; the modern town is Bad Hersfeld.
biblical_def: Hersfeld in Hesse was founded in 769 by Lull, the English disciple and successor of Boniface at Mainz, and became an imperial abbey with extensive lands and its own mint. Lambert of Hersfeld, writing in the 1070s, produced one of the most independent-minded chronicles of the investiture period. The great Romanesque abbey church, one of the largest in Germany, was burned by French troops in 1761 and stands roofless. Its sharpest moment came on 30 April 1521: Luther, travelling to the Diet of Worms under imperial safe conduct and under a papal excommunication that forbade him to preach, was received by the abbot with honour and preached in the abbey church at the monks' request. The dictionary records Hersfeld for that sermon, because it shows what the issue actually was. An abbot who disregarded a ban to hear a man expound Scripture had made a judgement about where authority lies. “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) is that judgement's warrant, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) its ground, and “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) the thing Luther would not stop doing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an interdict as a prohibition of the pope restraining divine offices; safe conduct as a convoy or guard to protect a traveller; a diet as an assembly of princes; excommunication as expulsion from the church; and a sermon as a discourse for religious instruction.
webster_full: INTERDICT, n. In the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, by which the clergy are forbidden to celebrate divine service.
SAFE-CONDUCT, n. That which gives a safe passage; a convoy or guard to protect a person in an enemy's country.
DIET, n. An assembly of princes or delegates for legislative or other business; as the diet of Worms.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church.
SERMON, n. A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman, for the purpose of religious instruction.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
corruption_summary: Hessian imperial abbey founded 769 by Lull, where Luther preached in April 1521 on his way to the Diet of Worms despite the ban.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the abbot of Hersfeld acted on. He let an excommunicate preach because the monks wanted to hear the Scriptures opened, and Luke commends exactly that priority, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — hearers who go to the text rather than to the verdict.

The live temptation is to make the episode a story about courage. It is a story about authority. God has appointed a means, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21), and laid a charge on the preacher that no ban lifts, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Luther's own account of his subject is Paul's, “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16).

pos: n. (the Weser abbey founded 822, base of the Scandinavian mission and of Widukind the chronicler)
etymology: From Corbeia nova, the new Corbie, after the Picard abbey from which its monks came.
biblical_def: Corvey on the Weser was founded in 822 by monks from Corbie in Picardy, with Carolingian patronage, as an outpost of Christian learning in newly conquered Saxony. Its Westwork, completed in 885, is the only substantially surviving Carolingian westwork in Germany. Corvey mattered most as a base for the northern mission: Ansgar, the apostle of the North, was a monk of Corbie and then of Corvey before he was sent to Denmark and Sweden in the 820s and 830s and became archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen. Widukind of Corvey wrote there in the 960s his history of the Saxons, and the abbey held a library whose catalogue once recorded a text of Tacitus. The dictionary records Corvey for Ansgar's sending, because the Scandinavian mission was undertaken with almost no prospect of success and persisted for decades. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) explains why it was attempted, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11) why it was continued, and “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is the word for men who saw little in their lifetimes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a westwork is given under west as the quarter where the sun sets; a chronicle as a register of events; a mission as a sending forth; the north as the northern region; and perseverance as persistence in a design.
webster_full: WEST, n. The point where the sun sets at the equinox, or any point in the same vertical direction.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
MISSION, n. A sending or delegating; persons sent; commission; the act of sending.
NORTH, n. One of the cardinal points, being that point of the horizon which is directly opposite to the sun in the meridian.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; continued pursuit of any business or enterprise begun.

Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Abbey founded on the Weser in 822 from Corbie, base of Ansgar's Scandinavian mission and home of Widukind the chronicler.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is obedience without visible return. Ansgar went north on the strength of a command, “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19), and saw his Swedish work largely undone in his own lifetime. Isaiah supplies the reason to keep going, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

The live temptation is to measure a mission by its statistics, which would have written off the ninth-century north entirely. Paul addresses himself to people in exactly that position, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9), and the charge does not vary with the response rate, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (the Ruhr abbey founded 799 by Liudger, missionary to the Saxons and first bishop of Munster)
etymology: Old Saxon werid, a river island or raised ground by water, on the Ruhr.
biblical_def: Werden on the Ruhr, now a district of Essen, was founded about 799 by Liudger, a Frisian trained under Gregory at Utrecht and then under Alcuin at York, who preached among the Frisians and the Saxons and became the first bishop of Munster. He died at Werden in 809 and was buried in its church, which remains as a fine late Romanesque building. The abbey held a famous psalter and a collection of Old Saxon material, and its estate records are among the earliest in the region. The dictionary records Werden for Liudger's training, which is an unusually clear case of how the mission to the Germans actually worked. A Frisian learned from an Englishman at York who had learned from Bede's tradition at Jarrow, and then went back to preach among the Saxons. “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) is the mechanism at every link, “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7) describes what each generation owed the last, and “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.” (Psa 145:4) is the shape of the whole.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms; a tradition as that delivered from father to son; succession as a following in order; discipleship is given under disciple as a learner; and a generation as a single succession.
webster_full: PSALTER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; the act of following in order; a series of persons or things.
DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
GENERATION, n. A single succession of natural descent, as the children of the same parents; a race.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Ruhr abbey founded about 799 by Liudger, trained at Utrecht and York, missionary to the Saxons and first bishop of Munster.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the chain of hearing. Liudger learned at York from men in Bede's tradition and preached to the Saxons, and Paul names the mechanism at every link: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Hebrews describes the debt each generation owes its teachers, “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7), and it is a debt of faith followed, not of office inherited.

The live temptation is to turn that chain into an institutional succession that guarantees truth. Hebrews ties it to the word spoken and the faith shown, not to a lineage. The Psalmist gives the shape, “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.” (Psa 145:4), and the duty at each stage is the plain “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (the Eifel abbey founded 721 and refounded by Pepin, where the emperor Lothair I died in 855)
etymology: From the river Pruem in the Eifel, of Celtic origin; the German spelling carries an umlaut not reproduced in the slug.
biblical_def: Prum in the Eifel was founded in 721 by the widow Bertrada and her son and refounded in 752 by Pepin the Short, who made it a royal abbey and endowed it richly; it became one of the chief Carolingian monasteries of the Rhineland. The emperor Lothair I abdicated and entered Prum as a monk in 855 and died there six days later. Its surviving treasure is documentary: the Liber Aureus, a cartulary of its charters, and the estate survey drawn up by the abbot Caesarius in 893, which is one of the best sources anywhere for the organisation of a Carolingian monastic estate — names, holdings, dues and services, parish by parish. The dictionary records Prum for the 893 survey, because the detail of it is a corrective to sentimentality about the period. The abbey was a landlord with tenants who owed labour. Scripture does not condemn an estate, and it does set a standard for how men under authority are treated: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) is the measure, and “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7) the dignity of the office that held the land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cartulary as a register of a monastery's charters; a survey as a determination of the contents of land; a tenant as one who holds lands of another; a due as that which is owed; and service as the performance of labour for another.
webster_full: CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; the place where records are kept.
SURVEY, n. The operation of finding the contour, dimensions and position of any part of the earth's surface.
TENANT, n. One who holds or possesses lands or other real estate, by any kind of right.
DUE, n. That which is owed; that which one contracts to pay, do or perform to another.
SERVICE, n. Labor of body or of body and mind, performed at the command of a superior.

Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Eph 2:9

Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Eifel royal abbey founded 721 and refounded by Pepin, whose estate survey of 893 documents a Carolingian monastic lordship in detail.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an institution holding land is answerable for how it treats the people on it. Prum's survey names tenants and their dues, and James supplies the measure for the holder of such a lordship, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27).

The live temptation is a romance about monastic economy as gentle and pre-commercial. The 893 register will not support it. The office that owned those fields had only the dignity Malachi gives it, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7), and a charge about souls, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28); the land conferred nothing extra, since “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) governs the abbot as the tenant.

pos: n. (the island abbey on Lake Constance founded 724, home of Walahfrid Strabo and Hermann the Lame)
etymology: German Reiche Au, the rich island or water-meadow; the Latin name is Augia dives.
biblical_def: Reichenau, an island in Lake Constance, was founded in 724 by Pirmin and became one of the great centres of Carolingian and Ottonian learning. Its scriptorium produced illuminated gospel books of the first rank, and its scholars are remembered individually: Walahfrid Strabo, abbot from 838, wrote the Hortulus, a poem on the plants of his garden, and commentaries long influential; and Hermann of Reichenau, called Hermann the Lame, who was severely disabled from birth and had to be carried, became in the eleventh century an astronomer, mathematician, music theorist and poet, and composed hymns still sung. Three Romanesque churches survive on the island. The dictionary records Reichenau above all for Hermann, because a man who could scarcely move produced work that outlasted every abbot who could. Scripture never makes usefulness a function of strength: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) is the rule, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) the prayer, and “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) the promise to a man whose labour looked impossible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scriptorium is given under scribe as a writer; astronomy as the science of the heavenly bodies; infirmity as an unsound state of body; a hymn as a song of adoration; and illumination as adornment with colours and gold.
webster_full: SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; a public writer; one who transcribes books.
ASTRONOMY, n. The science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions, distances and order.
INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To adorn with pictures or portraits, as a manuscript; to adorn with colors of various hues.

Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: Island abbey on Lake Constance founded 724, a great Carolingian scriptorium, home of Walahfrid Strabo and the disabled polymath Hermann the Lame.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God does not require strength to do His work. Hermann of Reichenau could not walk and wrote on the heavens and composed hymns, and Zechariah's word covers him precisely: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

The live temptation is to treat such a life as inspirational decoration rather than as theology. It is theology. The Psalmist's prayer is the one Hermann needed, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17), and Paul's promise is attached to labour without any qualification about capacity, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — with the exhortation that assumes exhaustion, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9).

pos: n. (the Hessian abbey founded 764, whose Carolingian gatehouse and cartulary survive)
etymology: From Latin Laurissa or Lauresham, of uncertain origin; the modern German form is contracted.
biblical_def: Lorsch in Hesse was founded in 764 by Count Cancor and his mother Williswinda, given to Chrodegang of Metz, and soon transferred to royal protection, becoming one of the richest abbeys of the Frankish world. Two things survive. The Torhalle, a small decorated gatehouse of about 800, is one of the very few substantially intact Carolingian buildings anywhere. And the Lorsch Codex, a cartulary compiled about 1170, preserves the texts of some three and a half thousand charters and is the principal source for the early medieval topography of the middle Rhine. A manuscript from Lorsch also carries the Lorsch Bee Blessing, a short Old High German charm for recovering a swarm, which mixes a prayer with an incantation. The dictionary records Lorsch for the bee charm, because it is a small honest window on what ordinary Christianity contained. Prayer over a lost swarm is entirely proper; an incantation is not, and the two sit in one text. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is the instrument for separating them, and “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) describes what prayer is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charm as words or characters imagined to possess occult power; an incantation as the act of using certain words to raise spirits; a swarm as a large number of bees; a cartulary as a register of charters; and a petition as a request to a superior.
webster_full: CHARM, n. Words, characters or other things imagined to possess some occult or unintelligible power.
INCANTATION, n. The act of enchanting; enchantment; the act of using certain words and ceremonies to raise spirits.
SWARM, n. A large number or body of small animals or insects, particularly when in motion.
CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; the place where records are kept.
PETITION, n. In a general sense, a request, supplication or prayer; a solemn or humble supplication.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Rich Hessian abbey founded 764, preserving the Carolingian Torhalle, a cartulary of some 3,500 charters, and the Old High German Bee Blessing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the line between prayer and charm, which the Lorsch bee text straddles in a few sentences. Prayer is petition to a Father who hears, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), and it is answered by Him rather than operated by the words. Paul hands the congregation the instrument for the separation, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).

The live temptation is to call such survivals quaint, as if a formula for compelling a result were not a different religion. Paul's warning names the mechanism, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8), a tradition of men grown into Christian practice, and Christ fixes the alternative, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24).

pos: n. (the Swabian abbey founded 764, converted into a noble canonry in 1460, site of a great witch persecution)
etymology: Old High German Elivangas, the elk meadows; the modern form keeps the plural.
biblical_def: Ellwangen in eastern Swabia was founded in 764 by two Alemannic nobles and became an imperial abbey. In 1460 it underwent a transformation common in late medieval Germany: at the request of its own members it was secularised into a collegiate foundation of canons, so that noblemen could hold its revenues without monastic vows, and its provost ruled the territory as a prince of the Empire. Ellwangen is also the site of one of the largest witch persecutions in Germany: between 1611 and 1618 several hundred people, most of them women, were tried by the provost's courts, convicted on confessions obtained under torture, and executed. The dictionary records both facts in one entry because they belong together. An institution that had converted the religious life into an income was also the court that burned its neighbours. Scripture's standards would have stopped it: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) requires examination rather than extraction, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) forbids the instrument, and “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) names the religion God actually accepts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canonry as the benefice of a canon; secularisation is given under secularise as conversion to common use; torture as extreme pain inflicted judicially; a confession as acknowledgment of a crime; and a sinecure as an office without duties.
webster_full: CANONRY, n. An ecclesiastical benefice, in a cathedral or collegiate church, which has a prebend or stated allowance.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To make secular; to convert from spiritual appropriation to secular or common use.
TORTURE, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; pain inflicted judicially, to extort a confession.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime or fault; avowal; the act of disclosing sins.
SINECURE, n. An ecclesiastical benefice, without cure of souls; an office which yields revenue without labor.

corruption_summary: Swabian imperial abbey of 764 secularised into a noble canonry in 1460, whose courts executed several hundred people for witchcraft from 1611 to 1618.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a confession extracted is not evidence. Paul's word for testing means examining a thing on its merits, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), and Zechariah forbids outright the power the Ellwangen courts used, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

The live temptation is to treat the persecution as the superstition of its age and the canonry as mere administrative untidiness. They were connected. A body that had turned its vocation into a revenue had no spiritual office left to restrain it, and the charge it had abandoned was “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28). The religion God accepts is James', “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27), and burning widows is its opposite.

pos: n. (the Swabian imperial abbey founded 764, rebuilt as one of the great Baroque churches)
etymology: Old High German Otinburra, Oto's dwellings; the modern form keeps both elements.
biblical_def: Ottobeuren in Swabia was founded in 764 and granted imperial immediacy by Charlemagne, making its abbot answerable to the emperor alone. It adopted the Hirsau reform in the eleventh century and kept a good school and library. Its fame rests on what it built in the eighteenth century: between 1737 and 1766 the abbey raised a vast Baroque basilica, designed finally by Johann Michael Fischer, with frescoes, stucco and three organs by Karl Joseph Riepp, which is among the supreme achievements of south German Baroque. The abbey still functions. The dictionary records Ottobeuren for that building, and states the Reformed judgement on it without pretending the question is easy. The church is magnificent, the music written for its organs is a real good, and “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8) licenses a Christian to say so. What the building also does is teach by overwhelming the senses, and the Reformed objection is not to beauty but to that substitution: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) names the appointed channel, and “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) refuses to let a room do the work of a heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Baroque is not in Webster, but ornament is defined as that which embellishes; a fresco as a painting on fresh plaster; an organ as the largest wind instrument; stucco as a fine plaster; and splendour as great brightness.
webster_full: ORNAMENT, n. That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
FRESCO, n. A method of painting in relief on walls, performed with water colors on fresh plaster.
ORGAN, n. The largest and most harmonious of wind instruments of music, blown with bellows.
STUCCO, n. A fine plaster, composed of lime, chalk and pulverized marble, used for walls and ceilings.
SPLENDOR, n. Great brightness; brilliant luster; magnificence; pomp; parade.

corruption_summary: Swabian imperial abbey of 764, rebuilt between 1737 and 1766 as one of the supreme achievements of south German Baroque.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Reformed objection is not to beauty. Paul tells Christians to think on whatever is true and lovely, “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8), and the music written for Ottobeuren's organs falls squarely inside that permission.

The live temptation is the substitution, where a room is built to do the convincing. Paul names the channel God appointed and it is auditory, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and Christ declines to locate worship in any building, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24). The aim is lodging the word in people, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16), which stucco cannot accomplish.

pos: n. (the Swabian abbey founded 1089 by the Hirsau reform, rebuilt in the Baroque)
etymology: German zwei Falten, the two folds or valleys, for its site between two streams.
biblical_def: Zwiefalten in Swabia was founded in 1089 by the counts of Achalm under the direction of monks from Hirsau, as part of the reform movement that carried Cluniac discipline through southern Germany. It had an unusually literate early community: Ortlieb and Berthold of Zwiefalten wrote chronicles of the house in the twelfth century that record its founding and early struggles in detail. Like Ottobeuren it was rebuilt in the eighteenth century, the church raised between 1739 and 1765 to designs by Johann Michael Fischer with decoration by the Feuchtmayer workshop, and it was dissolved in the secularisation of 1803. The dictionary records Zwiefalten for the pattern it completes. A house founded by reformers in 1089 to recover austerity ended as a Baroque church of extraordinary richness and then as state property. That sequence — reform, prosperity, display, dissolution — is the monastic cycle in four words, and it is why “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) rather than any new rule is Christ's prescription, with “hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11) beside it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines austerity as severity of manners; a reform as a change from worse to better; secularisation is given under secularise as conversion to common use; a chronicle as a register of events; and declension as a falling off.
webster_full: AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
REFORM, v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To make secular; to convert from spiritual appropriation to secular or common use.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
DECLENSION, n. A falling off; decay; a deviation from rectitude; a sinking into a lower state.

corruption_summary: Swabian abbey founded 1089 under the Hirsau reform, rebuilt in high Baroque between 1739 and 1765, dissolved in 1803.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the cycle repeats and a new rule never breaks it. Zwiefalten was founded to recover austerity and ended in gilt, and Christ's instruction to a declining church is not reorganisation but return: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), with “hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11) for the one still standing.

The live temptation is to look for a better institutional design. Seven centuries of German monastic reform is the experiment, and the result is on the ceiling at Zwiefalten. What Scripture offers instead is perseverance, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9), resting on a standing that no decline forfeits and no austerity earns, “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

pos: n. (the Black Forest abbey whose reform under Abbot William carried Cluniac discipline through Germany)
etymology: Old High German Hirz-owa, the stag's water-meadow, on the Nagold.
biblical_def: Hirsau in the northern Black Forest was refounded in 1065 and came under Abbot William, who governed from 1069 to 1091 and made it the centre of a German reform movement. The Hirsau constitutions adapted Cluniac practice to German conditions, insisted on the free election of abbots and freedom from lay proprietors, developed the institution of lay brothers, and were adopted by well over a hundred houses, Zwiefalten among them. Hirsau stood with the papacy during the investiture contest. The abbey was dissolved at the Reformation, converted into a ducal hunting lodge, and burned by French troops in 1692; the ruins with their great tower are a landmark of German Romanticism. The dictionary records Hirsau for the reform's central demand, which was right. Lay proprietors treating churches as property was a genuine abuse, and freedom from it is a proper aim. What Hirsau could not supply is the thing the Reformation added: a congregation with the text in hand. “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) is that addition, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) its authority, and “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) the duty it creates.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lay brother as one admitted for service without orders; investiture as the giving of possession of an office; election as the choice of a person for an office; proprietary as belonging to an owner; and discipline as instruction and government.
webster_full: LAY, a. Pertaining to the laity or people, in distinction from the clergy; not clerical.
INVESTITURE, n. The act of giving possession of a manor, office or benefice.
ELECTION, n. The act of choosing a person to fill an office or employment, by any manifestation of preference.
PROPRIETARY, n. A proprietor or owner; one who has the exclusive title to a thing.
DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; subjection to laws, rules, order, precepts or regulations.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
corruption_summary: Black Forest abbey whose reform under Abbot William, 1069 to 1091, carried adapted Cluniac discipline to more than a hundred German houses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Hirsau demand was just as far as it went. Churches held as a layman's property is an abuse, and freeing them was right. Christ's own reforming word is of that kind, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), a return to what was first done.

The live temptation is to think discipline is the whole of reformation. Hirsau reformed a hundred houses and left the people outside them exactly where they were. What the sixteenth century added was a congregation examining the text, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), on an authority located in the writings themselves, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), creating a duty no abbot can discharge for anyone, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).
